items.title: Apple ML Research releases MLX for local and distributed large language model inference on Mac Studio, demonstrating Muse Spark Open with nearly a trillion parameters [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Apple ML Research: Muse Spark Open with MLX on Mac Studio
items.summary:
Apple ML Research has introduced MLX, an open-source framework that enables local and distributed inference of large language models on Mac Studio with Apple silicon. The framework leverages unified memory architecture and supports models like Muse Spark Open, which has nearly a trillion parameters and can generate over 36 tokens per second on a cluster of four Mac Studios. Performance benchmarks compare the M5 Ultra and M3 Ultra Mac Studio generations, highlighting significant speed and efficiency improvements due to the GPU Neural Accelerator and increased memory bandwidth.

MLX supports running large models with extensive context sizes, such as 8,192 and 65,536 tokens, and demonstrates energy-efficient inference with peak power consumption around 200 to 300 watts. Muse Spark Open requires distributed memory across multiple Mac Studios due to its size, while smaller models like Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5 fit on a single Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM. This development allows AI researchers and developers to experiment with advanced models in private environments using Apple hardware.

items.title: StarSkirmish benchmark evaluates Gemini 4 Argon and other LLMs writing StarCraft bots in one hour, with GPT-6 Astra leading in performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Show HN: Gemini 4 Argon plays StarCraft
items.summary:
StarSkirmish is a benchmark where large language models (LLMs) write Protoss bots for StarCraft: Brood War in C++ within one hour, then compete against human-written bots and other LLM bots. The latest version, v0.2, includes flagship models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta, with Gemini 4 Argon placing third behind GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol. Scores reflect average win rates against a roster of competitive bots, highlighting the models' long-horizon reasoning and agentic coding capabilities.

The benchmark runs each model in its lab's command-line interface harness at the highest reasoning setting available, with practice games influencing final bot strength. Despite improvements, the strongest human-written bots remain well ahead, with GPT-6 Astra winning only 7% of games against top human bots. The results also show variability between runs, especially for Gemini 4 Argon, and emphasize the importance of practice against strong opponents during the development hour.

items.title: Vercel says Jev is its fastest-adopted AI model, used by 35% of paid teams within two weeks of launch [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Jev is Vercel’s fastest-adopted AI model ever
items.summary:
Jev, an AI model developed by TypeSafe AI, has become Vercel's fastest-adopted model, reaching 35% usage among paid teams within two weeks of its September 15 limited release. Designed as a lightweight decision model for selecting between predetermined outputs, Jev offers faster and cheaper processing compared to alternatives like Sonnet 5.5, making it suitable for classifying large data volumes quickly.

Vercel's data, sourced from its AI gateway API service, shows Jev nearly doubled the reach of the second most popular model and was adopted early by Vercel itself to replace GPT-6 Luna for harmful command classification. The report also highlights that open source models now process over 70% of tokens through Vercel's gateway and account for nearly 25% of total spending, while spending on frontier AI labs has grown tenfold, suggesting complementary growth between open source and frontier models.

The article discusses the evolution of AI image generation from rudimentary, often flawed outputs to more realistic but less distinctive creations. The author expresses nostalgia for the earlier, imperfect AI art that, despite its technical shortcomings, had a unique and surreal quality that modern models lack.

The piece highlights how advances in AI have led to more commercially viable images but at the cost of creativity and novelty, resulting in homogenized outputs that feel less like art and more like simulations. It also references specific AI models like DALL·E 2 and contrasts their outputs with newer versions, emphasizing the loss of the 'sound of failure' that once defined the medium's character.

items.originalTitle: Mark Wahlberg on using AI in film ‘the right way’ and being open to an AI clone carrying on his legacy
items.summary:
Actor and investor Mark Wahlberg expressed support for using AI in filmmaking to enhance production elements, such as stadium settings in his upcoming Pete Rose biopic, while emphasizing the importance of storytelling. He stated he opposes fully AI-generated scripts without real actors but welcomes AI as a tool to improve creative work.

Wahlberg also said he is open to creating an AI likeness of himself through technologies like CAA Vault, allowing his image and voice to be used in future projects by his descendants. He mentioned that an AI version of his character in the animated series "Ted" could continue beyond his active involvement, reflecting his interest in how AI might extend creative legacies.

items.originalTitle: China proposes export controls on AI technologies
items.summary:
China's Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology have proposed revisions to the country's export control list, adding 40 key technologies in artificial intelligence, biomedicine, and photovoltaics. The proposal includes 14 technologies banned from export and 26 subject to restrictions, with a focus on preventing misuse while supporting international cooperation and innovation.

The revisions aim to address security risks associated with AI-driven malicious code, gene therapy platforms, and photovoltaic manufacturing technologies, among others. The government plans to implement temporary pre-export registration measures and has outlined exemptions and facilitation policies to balance security with industry development. The updated controls will take effect upon formal announcement, with ongoing adjustments expected based on technological progress and industry feedback.

items.originalTitle: Postgres 19 delayed after AI reviewers find more bugs than humans can fix
items.summary:
The PostgreSQL Global Development Group has postponed the release of PostgreSQL 19 to around November 19, citing an unusually high number of bugs found by AI-assisted code reviews that exceed the development team's capacity to address before launch. Between eight and ten significant features have been reverted to the next release cycle, PostgreSQL 20, due to architectural defects and numerous minor issues uncovered by the new review process.

Peter Eisentraut, a leading PostgreSQL committer, explained that the improved AI tooling raised the quality bar by identifying many edge-case bugs earlier than traditional methods, resulting in a backlog of defect reports that could not be resolved in time. Despite the delay and feature rollbacks, PostgreSQL 19 will still include important updates like REPACK CONCURRENTLY and is expected to be robust after the additional scrutiny. The reverted features, including support for SQL Property Graph Queries, are likely to be included in PostgreSQL 20, which was initially planned as a bug-fix-only release.

items.summary:
Google Deepmind's Gemini 4 Argon model achieved a 97.5 percent score on the ARC-AGI-3 benchmark using a vendor-specific test setup, making it the second AI system after OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra to surpass 95 percent on this challenging general problem-solving test. However, in a standard testing environment with fewer features, Argon's score dropped to 49.8 percent, and it also lagged behind competitors in math and software engineering benchmarks.

The performance differences stem from varying test conditions, including the use of retained reasoning and context compaction features in the Provider Adapter Harness, which Argon leveraged. While Argon excelled in knowledge, agent, and vision tasks, it completed fewer games at higher reasoning levels and faced API limitations during testing. Research from Epoch AI places Argon close to top models on a combined capabilities index but highlights its relative weaknesses in specific domains compared to rivals.

items.originalTitle: OpenSpec: A task tracker with a spec attached?
items.summary:
A study analyzing 87 OpenSpec projects and 1,725 open changes found that while the format and grammar rules are mostly followed, many teams break OpenSpec's own writing guidelines, especially as specs grow larger. The research showed that only about 55% of requirements state a single obligation and just 35% include failure scenarios, with larger projects scoring worse due to bundling obligations and including implementation details. Additionally, 39% of open changes were fully ticked but not archived, indicating specs often do not reflect completed work and are used more like task trackers with attached specs.

The study also found no correlation between GitHub stars and spec quality, and that clarity and testability hold up regardless of project size, but atomicity and avoidance of implementation details decline in larger specs. Recommendations include automating writing rule checks in continuous integration, making archiving part of the definition of done, and maintaining English headings for tooling compatibility. The findings are based on correlations across public repositories analyzed with language models and reflect snapshots from October 2026.

Meta describes the update as a consolidation of existing policies rather than a change in crawling practices, but critics see it as a significant expansion of Meta's rights over third-party content.

items.summary:
Nick Cammarata, a researcher at Goodfire, challenges previous assumptions about neural network complexity in a new essay, suggesting that most neurons serve distinct, understandable roles rather than mixed or polysemantic functions. This reinterpretation questions earlier theories like superposition and proposes that improved tools and larger models reveal clearer neuron functions, potentially aiding AI safety efforts by making model behavior more transparent.

Cammarata's findings indicate that about 90% of neurons in models like Qwen3-32B have one main function, with only a small fraction remaining ambiguous. This clarity could help detect deception or dangerous behavior within AI models by allowing humans to read and understand internal circuits directly. While some experts hail this as a significant advance for AI alignment, others caution against overhyping the results, keeping the debate active within the research community.

items.summary:
The sentiment gap between public and private markets could not be wider right now. Wall Street investors have been increasingly worried about overborrowing by AI-related companies, as evidenced by skyrocketing yields on CoreWeave bonds, a selloff in semiconductor stocks and the yanking of the IPO of Firmus, the Australian data center operator.

Investors in private tech startups are still ebullient, blown away by how fast startups like Fireworks AI have grown. 

This bifurcation was evident to me this week at Morgan Stanley’s annual private tech companies conference. The mutual fund and other investors fanning out across a lush seaside resort in Dana Point, Calif., were aware of the red washing over trading screens. But that didn’t prevent them from rushing to meet the dozens of startup founders there, particularly if they were in the hot defense or inference sectors. 

“You can see there's a stark disconnect between the public markets and the private markets,” said Diana Doyle, Morgan Stanley’s head of technology equity and equity-linked capital markets on the sidelines of the conference.

items.summary:
It’s beginning to look like Anthropic waited too late to go public. Third-quarter revenue numbers disclosed to investors on Wednesday implied that its growth has slowed from the second quarter, which we reported is likely to put a ceiling on its IPO valuation. Anthropic might have been better off going public in June, when its growth was still spectacular. (Of course, a June IPO might have been impractical given that that’s when SpaceX went public.)

As things stand now, Anthropic’s slowing growth may remind investors of a longstanding question surrounding the company: How much of a moat does it really have? Yes, its AI models are as good as they get, but increasingly, businesses don’t need really expensive frontier models. As we wrote earlier this week, developers are increasingly opting for other models that are good enough for most tasks. Anthropic’s aggressive pricing has prompted companies such as Microsoft to cut its spending on the former’s models, we reported 10 days ago. (This trend seems to be spreading).

items.originalTitle: Why AI-Written Software Needs a Flight Simulator
items.summary:
As companies create more applications using AI, corporate officers say demand is rising for a new type of software that stress-tests those apps, simulating how they handle network problems and other disasters that humans may not think to test for—including cyberattacks by rogue AIs.

Luis Chávez, CTO of coding assistant provider Replit, says his company uses an AI-assisted software known as a deterministic simulator, a kind of flight simulator for software. The deterministic part refers to how the simulator lets companies run the same disaster test again and again so they can try out different fixes for bugs that crop up during network failures or hacking attempts.

Traditional stress-testing methods rely on developers guessing every potential problem that may arise. Merely using today’s AI models to evaluate code often produces false alarms or fake warnings, corporate executives say.

items.originalTitle: Cognition’s Plan to Limit Tokenmaxxing to the Most Efficient Engineers
items.summary:
To rein in AI spending, large companies are capping employees’ usage, turning to cheaper and smaller models and using routers to send only the hardest requests to the most expensive models.

Cognition, the startup behind the AI coding agent Devin, is adding a new trick to the book: measuring how efficiently different engineers use AI so companies can allocate more resources toward their most efficient employees, Cognition told The Information exclusively.

“The limits that a user should have should not be static. They should be dynamic based on the efficiency of your usage and the value that you're getting out of it,” said Calvin Giroud, a vice president of customer engineering at Cognition.

By looking at an engineer’s coding session using Devin, Cognition can estimate the equivalent number of hours it would have taken a human to do the same amount of work. Dividing by the costs of that session, Cognition gets a measure of each engineer’s efficiency.
